rw: Probability is a number that expresses how likely an event is to happen, running from 0 for impossible events up to 1 for certain events, so this definition is right.

ww.A measure of how clear a chart looks to: Chart clarity is a design and readability matter, not a measure of chance, so it describes presentation quality and has nothing to do with how likely an event is.
ww.A measure of how fast a computer runs ea: Computer speed is measured in operations per second or run time, which is a performance measure and has no connection to the chance of an event occurring.
ww.A measure of how large a group is in a t: The size of a group is a count or population figure, which tells you how many members there are but nothing about how likely any event is.

rw: A probability of 0 is the lowest possible value and means the event is impossible, so it cannot happen under the stated conditions at all.

ww.Is a coin toss: A coin toss with two equal outcomes has probability 0.5 for each side, not 0, so a probability of 0 does not describe a coin toss.
ww.Happens often: An event that happens often has a high probability, close to 1, so it is the opposite of an event with probability 0, which never occurs.
ww.Always happens: An event that always happens has probability 1, not 0, since 1 marks certainty while 0 marks impossibility, so this describes the opposite end of the scale.

rw: A probability of 1 is the highest possible value and means the event is certain, so it will happen every time under the stated conditions.

ww.Cannot happen at all: An event that cannot happen at all has probability 0, not 1, so this describes the opposite end of the probability scale from certainty.
ww.Happens by chance once: Happening by chance once is not a probability statement, and a single occurrence does not set the value; a probability of 1 means certainty, not one lucky event.
ww.Happens half the time: Happening half the time means a probability of 0.5, not 1, because 1 means the event occurs in every case rather than in half of them.

rw: A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes and heads is 1 of them, so the probability is 1 divided by 2, which equals 0.5.

ww.1: A probability of 1 means heads is certain on every toss, which is false for a fair coin that lands tails half the time, so 1 is wrong.
ww.2: A probability can never exceed 1, so a value of 2 is impossible; a fair coin has two equal outcomes, giving 1 out of 2 for heads.
ww.0.25: A value of 0.25 would be 1 chance in 4, but a coin has only 2 equal outcomes, so heads is 1/2 = 0.5 and not 0.25.

rw: There are 3 red marbles among 3 + 7 = 10 in total, so the probability of red is 3/10, which equals 0.3.

ww.3: A probability cannot be greater than 1, so 3 is impossible; the count of red marbles must be divided by the total of 10 to give a probability.
ww.0.37: The total is 3 + 7 = 10 marbles, so red is 3/10 = 0.3; the value 0.37 comes from wrongly joining the digits 3 and 7 together.
ww.0.7: The value 0.7 is the chance of drawing a blue marble, since 7 of the 10 marbles are blue, not red, so it answers a different question.

rw: Exactly one of the possible outcomes must occur, so the probabilities of all outcomes together cover the whole sample space and add up to 1, which is certainty.

ww.0: A sum of 0 would mean that no outcome can occur, but some outcome always happens, so the probabilities of all outcomes must add up to 1 and not 0.
ww.100: A sum of 100 would only apply if probabilities were written as percentages; as probabilities on a 0 to 1 scale, the total over all outcomes is 1, not 100.
ww.0.5: A sum of 0.5 would leave half the probability unassigned, but the possible outcomes cover every case, so their probabilities must add up to the full value of 1.

rw: Five of the six faces are not a six, so the probability of not rolling a 6 is 5/6, which is also 1 - 1/6.

ww.6/5: The fraction 6/5 equals 1.2, which is above 1, and no probability can exceed 1, so it cannot be the chance of avoiding a six.
ww.1/6: The fraction 1/6 is the chance of rolling a 6 itself, not of avoiding it, so it answers the opposite question; not rolling a 6 is 5/6.
ww.1/2: The fraction 1/2 would mean 3 of the 6 faces count as not-six, but 5 faces qualify, so the correct probability is 5/6 and not 1/2.

rw: Each coin lands heads with probability 1/2 and the tosses are independent, so both heads has probability 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

ww.1/2: The value 1/2 is the chance of one coin landing heads; both coins must land heads, so the probabilities multiply to 1/4, which is smaller than 1/2.
ww.2/4: The fraction 2/4 simplifies to 1/2, which is the chance for a single coin, whereas two heads in a row requires 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
ww.1/3: There are 4 equally likely outcomes (HH, HT, TH, TT) and only one is both heads, so the probability is 1/4, not 1/3.

rw: The mean is found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values, which gives the arithmetic average of the data set.

ww.The largest value minus the smallest val: The largest value minus the smallest value is the range, which measures spread, whereas the mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are.
ww.The middle value when the whole data is: The middle value of sorted data is the median, a different measure of center, and not the mean, which comes from adding all the values and dividing by their count.
ww.The value that appears most often in the: The value that appears most often is the mode, not the mean, because the mean uses every value in a sum and does not count frequency alone.

rw: After sorting the data from smallest to largest, the median is the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even.

ww.The value that appears most often in a s: The value that appears most often is the mode, a different measure; the median is found by sorting the data and taking the middle value.
ww.The difference between highest and lowes: The difference between the highest and lowest values is the range, which measures spread, not the middle of the data that the median describes.
ww.The sum of values divided by their count: The sum of the values divided by their count is the mean, a different average, which uses every value and is not the sorted middle value.

rw: The mode is the value that appears most often in a data set, so a set can have one mode, several modes, or none at all.

ww.The spread of the values in the set: The spread of values is described by the range or standard deviation, not the mode, which only identifies the most frequent value in the data.
ww.The middle value of the sorted data: The middle value of the sorted data is the median, not the mode, because the mode depends on how often values repeat and not on their position.
ww.The average of all of the values: The average of all the values is the mean, which comes from a sum divided by a count, while the mode is simply the most frequent value.

rw: Adding 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 gives 40, and dividing by the 5 values gives 40 / 5 = 8, which is also the middle value of this evenly spaced list.

ww.6: The sum is 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 40, and 40 / 5 = 8, so 6 is wrong; 6 is only the second value in the list.
ww.10: The value 10 is the fourth number in the list, not the average; the sum is 40 and 40 / 5 = 8, which is the actual mean.
ww.40: The value 40 is the sum of the five numbers and was not divided by the count of 5; dividing gives 40 / 5 = 8 for the mean.

rw: Sorted, the numbers are 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and with 5 values the middle one is the third, which is 5, so the median is 5.

ww.4: Sorting gives 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and 4 is the second value, not the middle one; with 5 values the median is the third value, which is 5.
ww.7: Sorted, the numbers are 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and 7 is the fourth value, one place past the middle; the median is the third value, 5.
ww.5.6: The value 5.6 is the mean, since 3 + 9 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 28 and 28 / 5 = 5.6, but the question asks for the median, which is 5.

rw: The range is the largest value minus the smallest value, which shows the total spread from the lowest point to the highest point in the data.

ww.The sum of all values in the data set: The sum of all values is found by adding them and gives a total, not a measure of spread; the range is the largest value minus the smallest.
ww.The most common value in the data set: The most common value is the mode, which measures frequency; the range instead measures spread by subtracting the smallest value from the largest value.
ww.The middle value of the whole data set o: The middle value of the data is the median, which measures center; the range measures spread by finding the gap between the extremes.

rw: The range is the largest score minus the smallest score, so 95 - 62 = 33, which shows how far apart the highest and lowest results are.

ww.75: The value 75 is the median (the middle of the five sorted scores), not the range; the range is 95 - 62 = 33.
ww.78: The value 78 is not the difference between any extremes; the range is the highest score minus the lowest, so 95 - 62 = 33, not 78.
ww.157: The value 157 comes from adding the largest and smallest, 95 + 62, but the range subtracts them, so 95 - 62 = 33.

rw: Standard deviation measures how far the values typically sit from the mean, so a small value means tightly clustered data and a large one means widely spread data.

ww.The most common value in the data set: The most common value is the mode, which is a measure of frequency; standard deviation instead describes how spread out the values are around the mean.
ww.How many values are in a set of numbers: The number of values in a set is the sample size or count, which has no part in standard deviation, as that measures spread around the mean.
ww.The middle of the data when it is sorted: The middle of sorted data is the median, a measure of center; standard deviation measures spread, which is a different property of the data set.

rw: A large standard deviation means the scores lie far from the mean on average, so Class B, with the larger value, has the more spread out scores.

ww.Class A scored higher on average: The question says both classes share the same mean, so neither scored higher on average; the standard deviation tells you about spread and not about the average.
ww.Class A's scores are more spread out: Class A has the small standard deviation, so its scores are clustered close to the mean and are less spread out, not more, than Class B's.
ww.Both classes have identical scores: Different standard deviations show that the score distributions differ, so the classes cannot have identical scores even though they share the same mean.

rw: In statistics a population is the entire group you want to learn about, such as all students in a country, whether or not everyone is measured.

ww.The number of people in a city only each: A population is not limited to counting people in a city; it is the whole group of interest, and a count of residents is just one possible example.
ww.The result of a survey taken in a town: The result of a survey is data, not a population; a population is the entire group you want to learn about, and a survey only draws from it.
ww.A small group chosen for the study sampl: A small group chosen for a study is a sample, not a population; the population is the whole group from which the sample comes.

rw: A sample is a subset taken from the population and used to draw conclusions about the whole, since measuring every member is often too costly or slow.

ww.A single value in a data set that is far: A single value far from the others is an outlier, not a sample; a sample is a group of observations drawn from the population.
ww.The entire group being studied and asked: The entire group being studied is the population, not the sample; a sample is only the part of that group that actually gets measured or asked.
ww.A chart of the findings of a survey in a: A chart of survey findings is a way of displaying results, not a sample; the sample is the set of people or items actually chosen and measured.

rw: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, which keeps the sample fair and makes it more representative of the whole group.

ww.It removes the need for any data to be c: Random sampling still requires data to be collected from the chosen members; it is a method for selecting who is measured and does not remove data collection.
ww.It lets the researcher pick favorites fr: Letting the researcher pick favorites introduces bias, which is exactly what random sampling avoids by making the choice depend on chance and not on preference.
ww.It guarantees the sample is the biggest: Random sampling does not guarantee the biggest possible sample; sample size is chosen separately, while randomness only decides who is picked, so this reason is wrong.

rw: Asking only students who eat in the cafeteria excludes those who bring lunch or eat elsewhere, so the sample is not representative, which is sampling bias.

ww.The data is too clean to be useful for t: Data being clean is a good thing and is not the problem here; the real flaw is that only cafeteria students are asked, which leaves other students out.
ww.The mean was calculated wrongly, using t: No mean has been calculated wrongly in this scenario; the flaw lies in who was asked, since students outside the cafeteria were never included in the survey.
ww.Too many questions asked of each student: The problem is not the number of questions per student; the problem is who was surveyed, since only cafeteria eaters were asked and everyone else was excluded.

rw: Correlation describes a relationship in which two variables tend to change together, whether both rise or one rises while the other falls, without implying a cause.

ww.A proof that one variable causes another: Correlation shows that variables move together but cannot prove that one causes the other, so describing it as proof of causation is a common mistake.
ww.A way of removing outliers from a data s: Removing outliers is a data-cleaning step and is unrelated to correlation, which measures how strongly two variables are linked to one another in the data.
ww.A random error in a data set that is cau: A random error caused by chance is noise or variance, not correlation, which is a pattern of two variables changing together in a consistent way.

rw: Both rise in summer because of a common cause, hot sunny weather, so they are correlated without ice cream causing sunburn, which is the best conclusion.

ww.Ice cream causes sunburn because of the: Sugar in ice cream does not cause sunburn; sunburn comes from ultraviolet sun exposure, so the shared rise in summer is not evidence that one causes the other.
ww.Sunburn causes ice cream sales as burned: Burned people do not drive ice cream sales in any meaningful way; both rise because summer heat and sun act as a third factor, not because one causes the other.
ww.The data must be wrong because both cann: Two variables can easily rise together when a common factor like summer weather drives both, so the data is not wrong, and this claim is false.

rw: A normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped curve in which most values cluster near the mean and fewer values appear farther out in the tails.

ww.A curve with all of the values equal to: If all values were equal there would be no spread at all, but a normal distribution is a bell curve with values spread around the mean.
ww.A straight line rising steadily over the: A straight rising line is a linear trend over time and is not a distribution of values, so it does not describe a normal distribution.
ww.A scatter of random points that shows no: A random scatter with no pattern is not a normal distribution, which has a clear symmetric bell shape with values concentrated around the mean.

rw: By the empirical rule, about 68% of values in a normal distribution fall within one standard deviation of the mean, on both sides combined.

ww.About 95%: About 95% is the share within two standard deviations of the mean, not one; within one standard deviation the figure is roughly 68%.
ww.About 50%: The 50% figure is the share of values above or below the mean alone; within one standard deviation on both sides it is about 68%.
ww.About 100%: A share of 100% would require infinitely wide limits, because a normal curve has tails that extend outward; within one standard deviation it is about 68%.

rw: A hypothesis is a claim about a population that can be tested with data, such as saying the average height is 170 cm.

ww.A chart showing the results of a survey: A chart of results is a visualization, not a hypothesis; a hypothesis is a claim about a population that data can be used to test.
ww.A proven fact that needs no testing, fro: A hypothesis is not a proven fact; it is a statement that may be supported or rejected by data, so it must be open to testing.
ww.A sample of the population chosen at ran: A random sample of the population is data collected for study, not a hypothesis, which instead is a testable claim about the population itself.

rw: A small p-value means data this extreme would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, which is evidence against the null hypothesis, not proof of it.

ww.The sample is too small to use in any re: A p-value does not measure sample size; a small p-value means the observed result would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, not that the sample is too small.
ww.The null hypothesis is certainly true an: A small p-value points away from the null hypothesis being true and does not show that the result is chance; it suggests the result would be rare under that null.
ww.The data has no errors of any kind in it: A p-value says nothing about whether the data is free of errors; it only measures how surprising the result would be if the null hypothesis were true.

rw: A confidence interval is a range of values, calculated from sample data, that is likely to contain the true value of the population measure.

ww.The most common value in a sample drawn: The most common value in a sample is the mode, which is a single summary number, whereas a confidence interval is a range built around an estimate.
ww.The time needed to collect data from the: The time needed for collecting data has nothing to do with a confidence interval, which is a statistical range for an estimate and not a duration.
ww.A guarantee that the estimate is exact a: A confidence interval does not guarantee exactness; it reflects uncertainty by giving a range, and the true value could still lie outside the interval.

rw: Exploratory data analysis uses summaries and charts to understand the data, spot patterns, and find problems like missing values or outliers before building a model.

ww.Training a model on all of the data and: Training and testing on the same data is a modeling mistake that hides overfitting, whereas exploratory analysis means examining data to find patterns and problems.
ww.Publishing the final report to the publi: Publishing a final report is the last stage of a project, after the exploration is done, and does not describe examining data to find patterns.
ww.Deleting data that looks unusual without: Deleting unusual data without checking why is poor practice; exploratory analysis investigates unusual values first, to learn whether they are errors or real signals.

rw: A histogram groups values into ranges, called bins, and shows how many fall in each, so it reveals the shape of a distribution.

ww.To show the parts of a whole as slices o: Slices of a circle describe a pie chart, which shows parts of a whole, whereas a histogram shows how values are distributed across ranges.
ww.To show how two variables move together: Showing how two variables move together over time calls for a line or scatter chart, not a histogram, which displays a single variable's distribution.
ww.To show a list of exact names and values: Listing exact names and values is the job of a table, not a histogram, which summarizes counts in ranges with bars rather than listing individual entries.

rw: A scatter plot places each observation as a point using two numeric variables on the axes, so patterns such as trends or clusters in their relationship show clearly.

ww.A word cloud: A word cloud displays word frequency by text size and does not plot two numeric variables against each other, so it cannot show their relationship.
ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of a single whole, not the relationship between two numeric variables, so it cannot display how one changes with the other.
ww.A table of text: A table of text lists words and values without plotting them, so it makes the relationship between two numeric variables hard to see at a glance.

rw: A line chart connects points in time order, which makes rises, falls and trends over time easy to see, so it is the best choice here.

ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts at one moment and has no time axis, so it cannot display change over time.
ww.A scatter plot: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, and while it can show time on an axis, a line chart shows the trend more clearly.
ww.A histogram plot: A histogram displays how values are distributed in ranges and has no time axis, so it does not show how a value changes over time.

rw: Feature scaling adjusts numeric values, for example by normalizing to 0 through 1, so that features have comparable ranges and none dominates the model unfairly.

ww.Removing every column from the data set: Removing columns would reduce the features available and does not change numeric ranges; feature scaling adjusts values so features share comparable ranges.
ww.Making a chart larger on the screen for: Making a chart larger changes how it looks on screen and has no effect on the data values, whereas feature scaling adjusts numeric values in the data itself.
ww.Increasing the number of rows in a table: Adding rows changes the amount of data, not the range of values; feature scaling transforms the numbers in each column so that their ranges are comparable.

rw: A feature is an input variable that describes each example, such as the size of a house, and the model uses these inputs to learn patterns.

ww.The final answer a model predicts after: The final answer a model predicts is the label or target, not a feature; features are the inputs that the model uses to make that prediction.
ww.The computer a model runs on at the firm: The computer a model runs on is hardware, not a feature; in a data set, a feature is a column that describes each example.
ww.The name of the data file saved on a har: The name of a data file is metadata about storage and is not a feature, which is a variable that describes each example for the model.

rw: In supervised learning the label, or target, is the correct answer attached to each training example, and the model learns to predict it from the features.

ww.A chart legend that explains the colors: A chart legend explains colors in a graph and has nothing to do with learning; a label in supervised learning is the correct answer for each example.
ww.A comment typed by a programmer in the c: A comment typed in code is documentation for programmers, not a label; in supervised learning, a label is the correct answer the model learns to predict.
ww.An input column describing each example: An input column describing each example is a feature, not a label; the label is the output value the model is trained to predict.

rw: The sale price is what the model is trying to predict from the other columns, so it is the label (target), while the others serve as features.

ww.The square footage: Square footage is an input that describes a house and helps predict the price, so it is a feature and not the label being predicted.
ww.The bedroom count: Bedroom count describes the house and is used as an input to predict price, which makes it a feature rather than the label.
ww.The year built: The year built is another input describing the house that helps estimate price, so it is a feature, whereas the price itself is the label.

rw: A test set holds data the model never saw during training, so scoring on it shows how well the model works on new data and reveals overfitting.

ww.To avoid using labels at all in the mode: Splitting data does not remove the need for labels, since both training and test sets keep their labels so that predictions can be checked against true answers.
ww.To remove all outliers automatically fro: Splitting does not remove outliers; outlier handling is a separate cleaning step, while the split exists to test the model on unseen data.
ww.To make the data set smaller so it takes: The purpose of the split is not to save disk space; both parts together hold the same data, so the total size is unchanged.

rw: A big gap between 99% on training data and 60% on test data shows the model memorized training examples and fails to generalize, which is overfitting.

ww.Underfitting: Underfitting means poor results on both training and test data, but here training accuracy is high at 99%, so underfitting does not fit this pattern.
ww.Faster training: Faster training is about computation time and says nothing about the gap between 99% on training data and 60% on test data.
ww.A perfect model: A perfect model would score well on test data too; 60% on unseen data is far from perfect, so the model does not generalize and is not perfect.

rw: Poor results on both training and test data mean the model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data, which is underfitting.

ww.Overfitting: Overfitting gives high scores on training data and low scores on test data, but here both scores are poor, so overfitting is not the problem.
ww.Perfect accuracy: Perfect accuracy would mean high scores, but the model performs poorly on both sets, so this cannot describe the situation in the question.
ww.Data leakage: Data leakage usually makes test scores look unrealistically good, because test information slips into training, so it does not explain poor results on both sets.

rw: Accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by the total number of predictions, so it is the share of predictions that are correct.

ww.The size of the model file on the disk: The size of the model file on disk is a storage measure and does not reflect how many predictions are correct, which is what accuracy measures.
ww.The time a model takes to make its predi: The time a model takes to predict is speed or latency, not accuracy, which is about how many predictions turn out to be correct.
ww.The number of features used in the model: The number of features is a property of the input data, not a measure of quality; accuracy is the share of correct predictions.

rw: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions, so 90 / 120 = 0.75, which is 75%.

ww.30%: The value 30% is the share of errors in the other direction only if misread; the actual error rate is 30 / 120 = 25%, and accuracy is 75%.
ww.120%: An accuracy of 120% is impossible because it cannot exceed 100%; the calculation 90 / 120 gives 0.75, which is 75%.
ww.90%: The number 90 is the count of correct predictions, not a percentage; dividing by 120 predictions gives 90 / 120 = 75% as the accuracy.

rw: If 99% of cases belong to one class, a model that always predicts that class is right 99% of the time while never finding the rare class.

ww.Accuracy always equals 50% in a data set: Accuracy does not always equal 50% in skewed data; its value depends on how many predictions are correct, and it can be misleadingly high.
ww.Accuracy cannot be calculated when the c: Accuracy can still be calculated with unbalanced classes; the problem is that the number can look high without the model detecting the rare class.
ww.Rare classes are never important, so a m: Rare classes are often the most important, such as fraud or disease, so saying they are never important is false and is not why accuracy misleads.

rw: A confusion matrix is a table with predicted classes on one axis and actual classes on the other, showing correct predictions and the types of errors.

ww.A list of all of the training data used: A list of all training data is just the data set; a confusion matrix is a table that compares predicted classes with actual classes.
ww.A table of confusing column names in the: A confusion matrix is not about confusing column names; it counts how often the model confuses one class for another in its predictions.
ww.A chart of the weather in the region ove: A chart of the weather over a year has nothing to do with evaluating a model; a confusion matrix tabulates predicted against actual classes.

rw: A false positive occurs when the model predicts yes but the true answer is no, which means it raised a false alarm.

ww.The model predicts no and is right about: Predicting no and being right is a true negative, since both the prediction and the reality are negative, so it is not a false positive.
ww.The model predicts no, but the true answ: Predicting no when the true answer is yes is a false negative, a missed case, which is the opposite error of a false positive.
ww.The model predicts yes and is right abou: Predicting yes and being right is a true positive, because the prediction matches reality, so it is a correct result and not a false positive.

rw: A false negative occurs when the model predicts no but the true answer is yes, which means the model missed a real positive case.

ww.The model predicts no and is right about: Predicting no and being right is a true negative, since the prediction matches reality, so this is a correct result and not a false negative.
ww.The model predicts yes and is right abou: Predicting yes and being right is a true positive, a correct outcome, so it cannot be a false negative, which is a missed positive case.
ww.The model predicts yes, but the true ans: Predicting yes when the true answer is no is a false positive, a false alarm, which is the opposite error of a false negative.

rw: Precision is the share of cases predicted positive that really are positive, so it shows how trustworthy the model's positive predictions are.

ww.Of all real positives in the data, how m: Finding all the real positives in the data describes recall, not precision; precision looks only at the cases the model predicted as positive.
ww.How many features the model uses in its: The number of features is about the model's inputs and does not measure how reliable its positive predictions are, which is what precision measures.
ww.How fast the model runs on a computer at: Speed of the model is a performance measure for run time and has nothing to do with correctness of positive predictions, which precision measures.

rw: Recall is the share of all real positives that the model found, so a high recall means few real positive cases were missed.

ww.How long the model takes to train on the: Training duration is about time and cost, not about finding positives; recall measures how many of all real positives the model manages to find.
ww.Of predicted positives, how many were co: The share of predicted positives that are correct is precision, which looks at predictions; recall instead looks at the real positives in the data.
ww.How much memory the model uses to run it: Memory use is a resource measure and says nothing about how many real positive cases the model finds, which is what recall measures.

rw: Regression predicts a numeric value, such as a price or a temperature, which is why it is used for continuous outcomes.

ww.The best chart type for showing the resu: The best chart for results is a visualization decision, not something a regression model predicts; regression predicts a numeric value.
ww.A category such as spam or not spam for: Predicting a category like spam or not spam is classification, not regression, which outputs numbers rather than classes.
ww.A group of similar customers in a market: Grouping similar customers is clustering, an unsupervised task, whereas regression predicts a numeric value from input features.

rw: Classification predicts a category or class for each example, such as spam or not spam, so the output is a label from a fixed set.

ww.The time of day at which the data is col: The time of day data was collected is a detail about the data, not a prediction target type; classification predicts a category or class.
ww.A new random data set of unlabeled recor: Classification does not generate new random data sets; it assigns each input to a category, such as spam or not spam.
ww.A continuous number like income or a hou: Predicting a continuous number like income or a house price is regression, not classification, which instead assigns inputs to categories.

rw: Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks that usually need human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images and making decisions.

ww.Software that only edits photographs by: Photo editing by hand is a manual creative task and does not describe AI, which means systems that perform tasks needing human intelligence.
ww.Machines that only store large amounts o: Storing and printing files is basic data handling and does not involve reasoning or learning, so it does not define artificial intelligence.
ww.Any computer connected to the internet t: Being connected to the internet describes networking, and many connected computers use no AI at all, so this does not define AI.

rw: Machine learning is one approach to building AI in which systems learn patterns from data, so ML is a subset of the wider field of AI.

ww.Machine learning is the broader field th: This reverses the relationship: AI is the broader field and machine learning is one part of it, not the other way around.
ww.AI only works with images while ML only: Neither field is restricted to a single data type; both AI and ML work with images, text, numbers and audio, so this claim is false.
ww.They mean exactly the same thing in ever: The terms are related but not identical, because machine learning is only one method within AI, and other methods such as rule-based systems also exist.

rw: Narrow, or weak, AI is designed to do one specific task well, such as recognizing faces or recommending movies, and cannot move freely to unrelated tasks.

ww.AI that can do any task a human can do: An AI that can do any task a human can do is general AI, not narrow AI, which is built for one specific task.
ww.AI that is too small to be useful at all: Narrow AI is not defined by size or usefulness; many narrow systems are very useful and powerful at their one task, so this definition is wrong.
ww.AI that has human feelings and goals: Human feelings and goals describe a hypothetical conscious machine, which does not exist; narrow AI is simply focused on one task without feelings.

rw: General AI, or AGI, is a hypothetical system that could learn and perform any intellectual task a human can, and no such system exists today.

ww.An AI used by the military to guide dron: Military use describes where an AI might be applied, not what general AI is, which is defined by its ability to do any intellectual task.
ww.An AI freely available online to anyone: Free online availability concerns access and cost, not capability, so it does not define general AI, which is about broad human-level ability.
ww.An AI designed for only one task, such a: An AI built for one task such as chess or sorting mail is narrow AI, which is the opposite of general AI.

rw: A system that recommends movies from viewing history is built for one specific task, which makes it an example of narrow AI.

ww.A printer that prints a page from a comp: A printer that prints a file follows fixed instructions and does not learn or reason, so it is ordinary machinery and not narrow AI.
ww.A calculator that adds two numbers and s: A calculator performs fixed arithmetic with set rules and no learning or judgment, so it is not usually counted as AI at all.
ww.A machine that can do every human job as: A machine that can do every human job would be general AI, which is hypothetical, not narrow AI, which handles one specific task.

rw: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, such as a recipe a computer can follow.

ww.A random list of words used in a diction: A random list of words is not a procedure; an algorithm is a precise set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem.
ww.A type of computer screen used to displa: A computer screen is hardware for displaying output, whereas an algorithm is a sequence of instructions that solves a problem.
ww.A file that stores photos taken with a p: A file storing photos is data storage and not a set of instructions, so it does not describe an algorithm.

rw: A model in machine learning is the result of training an algorithm on data, and it holds the learned patterns used to make predictions.

ww.The data used to train and test the algo: The data used to train and test is the data set, not the model; the model is what you get after training an algorithm on data.
ww.A person who tests software for bugs and: A person who tests software is a tester, not a model; in machine learning, a model is the trained system that makes predictions.
ww.A toy version of a computer made for chi: A toy version of a computer for children has no relation to machine learning, where a model is the output of training an algorithm.

rw: Training means feeding data to an algorithm so that it learns patterns, producing a model that can then be used to make predictions.

ww.Teaching employees how to use a new prog: Teaching employees to use a program is staff training, which is a different meaning of the word and unrelated to machine learning.
ww.Deleting old data from the system to fre: Deleting old data to free space is housekeeping, and it does not teach an algorithm anything, so it is not training in machine learning.
ww.Printing the model's results on paper fo: Printing results on paper is reporting, and it does not help an algorithm learn; training in machine learning means learning patterns from data.

rw: Inference, or prediction, means using an already trained model to make a prediction on new data it has not seen before.

ww.Collecting the first data set used to tr: Collecting the first data set is part of data preparation before training, not inference, which means using a trained model on new data.
ww.Cleaning errors from data before it is u: Cleaning errors from data is a preparation step done before training, and it does not involve making predictions, so it is not inference.
ww.Building the model's code in a programmi: Writing the model's code is development work and not inference, which happens after the model is trained and is used to predict.

rw: A chatbot is a program that talks with users through text or voice, answering questions or carrying out requests in a conversation.

ww.A tool for editing spreadsheets and char: A tool for editing spreadsheets and charts is analysis software, not a chatbot, which is a program that converses with users.
ww.A robot that cleans floors in homes and: A robot that cleans floors is a household machine and not a chatbot, which is software that carries on a conversation.
ww.A device that stores passwords for your: A device that stores passwords is a password manager, which is a security tool and not a chatbot that holds conversations.

rw: A recommendation system uses data about users and items to suggest things a user may like, such as movies, songs or products.

ww.A system that prints personal letters fo: Printing personal letters is a document task and does not involve suggesting items, which is what a recommendation system does.
ww.A system that deletes unused files from: Deleting unused files is storage cleanup and does not suggest anything to users, so it is not a recommendation system.
ww.A system that blocks all advertisements: Blocking advertisements is the job of an ad blocker, which is the opposite of suggesting items a user may like.

rw: Automation means using technology to perform tasks with little human input, such as a machine sorting parcels or software sending routine messages.

ww.Doing every task by hand with no help fr: Doing every task by hand with no help from machines is manual work, which is the opposite of automation.
ww.Storing data in the cloud for use at a m: Storing data in the cloud is a storage practice and does not mean machines perform tasks with little human input, as automation does.
ww.Writing a program in a notebook by hand: Writing a program by hand in a notebook is just a way of drafting code and does not itself perform any task automatically.

rw: Sorting thousands of emails into categories is repetitive, high-volume and rule-driven, which suits AI very well and saves human time.

ww.Comforting a grieving customer in person: Comforting a grieving customer needs human empathy and presence, which AI cannot truly offer, so it is a poor candidate for automation.
ww.Choosing a company's mission and its cor: Choosing a mission and core values calls for human judgment about purpose and ethics, so it is not a good task for AI automation.
ww.Deciding whether a new law is fair to ci: Deciding whether a law is fair involves moral reasoning and social values, which should rest with people, so AI is a poor fit.

rw: Natural language processing is AI that helps computers understand and use human language, for example in translation, chatbots and text summaries.

ww.AI that helps computers store text files: Storing text files on a disk is a file storage task and does not involve understanding language, which is what NLP is for.
ww.AI that helps computers recognize faces: Recognizing faces in photos is computer vision, which works with images, whereas NLP works with human language in text and speech.
ww.AI that helps computers move robots in a: Moving robots on a factory line is robotics and control, which is a different area from NLP, which handles human language.

rw: Computer vision is AI that enables computers to interpret images and video, for example by recognizing objects, faces or text in pictures.

ww.AI that improves screen brightness on a: Improving screen brightness is a display feature and has no relation to interpreting what is in images, which is computer vision.
ww.AI that enables computers to speak in a: Speaking in a natural voice is speech synthesis, a language task, not computer vision, which deals with images and video.
ww.AI that checks eyesight in people at an: Checking eyesight at an eye clinic is a medical test of human vision and does not describe AI that interprets images.

rw: Speech recognition converts spoken words into text, which lets voice assistants and dictation tools understand what a person has said.

ww.Converting video into audio only: Converting video to audio is a media conversion that does not turn speech into text, so it is not speech recognition.
ww.Converting images into text files: Converting images into text files describes optical character recognition, which reads text from pictures and not from spoken audio.
ww.Converting text into spoken words: Converting text into spoken words is speech synthesis, or text-to-speech, which is the reverse of speech recognition.

rw: Generative AI creates new content such as text, images or music, based on patterns it learned from its training data.

ww.AI that only counts items in a table and: Counting items and reporting totals is basic data summarizing and does not create anything new, which is what generative AI does.
ww.AI that only sorts existing files into f: Sorting existing files into folders organizes content already there, whereas generative AI produces new content such as text or images.
ww.AI that only deletes duplicate data from: Deleting duplicate data is data cleaning and does not create new content, so it does not describe generative AI.

rw: A large language model is trained on huge amounts of text, which lets it generate and understand language, answer questions and write content.

ww.A device that records speech and plays i: A device that records and plays back speech is an audio recorder and has nothing to do with a language model trained on text.
ww.A program that translates one language i: Translating at borders describes a translation service and not an LLM, which is a model trained on huge amounts of text.
ww.A dictionary stored in a database of wor: A dictionary lists words and meanings and cannot generate new text, whereas an LLM learns language patterns from huge text collections.

rw: A hallucination is a confident answer that is false or made up, such as an invented fact or a citation to a source that does not exist.

ww.A very fast response from the system to: A fast response is about speed and says nothing about accuracy, whereas a hallucination is a confident answer that is false or made up.
ww.A correct answer with sources cited in f: A correct answer with sources cited is reliable output, which is the opposite of a hallucination, where the answer is false.
ww.A request to restart the system when it: A request to restart the system is a technical prompt or error message and has nothing to do with the false content of a hallucination.

rw: A prompt is the input or instruction given to an AI system, such as a question or a task description, that tells it what to do.

ww.The data used to train the AI before use: The data used to train the AI is its training data, which is provided before use, while a prompt is the input given at use.
ww.The code that runs the AI on a large ser: The code that runs the AI is the software, not the prompt, which is just the text or instruction that a user supplies.
ww.The final answer an AI gives back to the: The final answer an AI gives back is the output or response, not the prompt, which is the input the user provides.

rw: This prompt names the task (summarize), the format (three bullet points) and the audience (a high school student), giving clear detail that leads to a useful answer.

ww.Do the thing that I asked about earlier: Do the thing I asked earlier gives no content or context, so the model cannot know the task and the answer is unlikely to be useful.
ww.Write something about the topic that you: Write something about the topic is vague, with no subject, length or format, so the model must guess and the answer may not be useful.
ww.Tell me something interesting about anyt: Tell me something interesting about anything is open-ended with no goal, format or audience, so the response is unfocused and may not help the reader.

rw: The Turing test checks whether a machine can behave so much like a human in conversation that people cannot tell the difference, which is the standard test of machine intelligence.

ww.A test of how much data a model can stor: Storage capacity and disk speed are hardware measures, whereas the Turing test checks whether a machine's behavior can pass for human behavior.
ww.A test of how fast a computer processes: Processing speed is measured with benchmarks, not the Turing test, which is about whether a machine can imitate a human so well that it is indistinguishable.
ww.A test of a computer's memory size and h: Memory size and screen refresh rate are hardware specifications, and neither relates to the Turing test, which judges whether a machine can pass as human.

rw: One real benefit of AI for businesses is faster analysis of large amounts of data, which saves time and can reveal useful patterns.

ww.Guaranteed correct decisions in all case: AI can make mistakes and carries bias or errors, so decisions are never guaranteed correct in all cases, and this claim is false.
ww.Freedom from all costs of any kind in a: AI adds costs for data, computing power and expertise, so it does not free a firm from all costs, and this claim is false.
ww.Removal of any need for human oversight: Businesses still need human oversight to check AI results and handle errors, so AI does not remove that need, and this claim is false.

rw: A real limitation of current AI is that its performance depends on the quality of its training data, since poor or biased data leads to poor results.

ww.They never make mistakes of any kind in: AI systems do make mistakes, including wrong or biased outputs, so saying they never err is false and is not a limitation statement.
ww.They need no data to learn how to do a t: AI systems learn from data, so they cannot learn a task well with no data; this statement is false, though it is phrased as an ability.
ww.They understand every situation like a h: AI does not truly understand every situation as a human does; it finds patterns in data, so this claim is false and is not a fact.

rw: An expert system uses rules gathered from human experts to make decisions or give advice in a specific field, such as medical diagnosis.

ww.A program that stores files only and can: A program that only stores files cannot make decisions, so it is a storage tool and not an expert system, which applies expert rules to decide.
ww.A program that generates random music fo: Generating random music for a game is a creative generation task and does not apply expert knowledge, so it is not an expert system.
ww.A program that learns only from raw imag: An expert system relies on rules from human experts, whereas learning only from raw images with no expert rules describes a different kind of system.

rw: A rule-based system follows explicit if-then rules written by people, so its behavior is predictable and easy to trace to a specific rule.

ww.A system that learns its own rules from: Learning its own rules from data describes machine learning, whereas a rule-based system follows rules that people have written in advance.
ww.A system with no instructions at all and: A system with no instructions and no logic could not operate, so it cannot be a rule-based system, which depends on explicit rules.
ww.A system that changes its rules randomly: A rule-based system follows fixed rules, so it behaves predictably; changing rules at random each run is the opposite of how it works.

rw: A robot is a machine that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do and act, often by following programs that control its movements.

ww.Any computer connected to the internet,: A laptop, phone or server is a computer connected to the internet, but it does not sense and act physically, so it is not a robot.
ww.A screen that displays charts and tables: A screen that displays charts and tables is an output device that shows information and does not sense, decide or act as a robot does.
ww.A program that only stores data and cann: A program that only stores data and cannot act is not a robot, which must be able to take actions in the physical world.

rw: The Internet of Things means everyday devices, such as thermostats, watches and appliances, that are connected to the internet and share data.

ww.A kind of social media account used to p: A social media account for posting photos is a service for people, whereas the Internet of Things links physical devices that exchange data.
ww.A list of websites that are saved as boo: A list of bookmarked websites is a browser feature and not a network of connected devices, which is what the Internet of Things is.
ww.A network of only large computers kept i: The Internet of Things includes small everyday devices like sensors and appliances, so a network of only large data center computers does not describe it.

rw: AI learns by finding patterns, and the more varied examples it sees, the better it can learn those patterns and generalize to new cases.

ww.Data lets the computer avoid power: Data does not let a computer avoid power; AI training actually uses a lot of electricity, so this reason is wrong.
ww.Data makes the computer run cooler: Data does not cool the computer; the heat comes from processing, so a bigger data set tends to increase the workload.
ww.Data replaces the need for algorithms: Data does not replace algorithms, because an algorithm is still needed to learn from the data; both are required for machine learning.

rw: A spreadsheet organizes, calculates and analyzes data in rows and columns, using formulas and functions to total values or find averages.

ww.Sending video calls to coworkers across: Video calls are made with conferencing software, not a spreadsheet, which is a tool for working with data in rows and columns.
ww.Protecting computers from viruses and ot: Protecting computers from viruses is the job of security software, not a spreadsheet, which organizes and analyzes data.
ww.Editing photographs for a website and ma: Editing photographs is done with image-editing software, and a spreadsheet is designed for working with data in rows and columns instead.

rw: SUM adds all the numbers in a range, for example =SUM(A1:A10), which makes it the right function for finding a total.

ww.COUNT: COUNT tells you how many cells contain numbers, not their total, so it does not add the values together as SUM does.
ww.MAX: MAX returns the largest value in a range and does not add numbers, so it cannot give the total of the range.
ww.IF: IF tests a condition and returns one of two results, so it is a logic function and does not add a range of numbers.

rw: AVERAGE adds the numbers in a range and divides by how many there are, so it returns the mean of the range.

ww.MIN: MIN returns the smallest value in the range, not the average, so it does not describe the center of the data.
ww.SUM: SUM adds all the values in a range to give a total, and without dividing by the count it is not the average.
ww.ROUND: ROUND changes a number to a chosen number of decimal places and does not calculate any average of a range.

rw: COUNTIF counts the cells in B2:B10 that equal the word Yes, so it returns the number of cells in the range that match.

ww.An error because the word Yes is only te: COUNTIF accepts text criteria, so the word Yes works fine and does not cause an error; it counts the cells that match.
ww.The sum of the cells in the range B2 to: Summing the cells would need the SUM function; COUNTIF counts matching cells and does not add up their values.
ww.The word Yes repeated nine times in a co: COUNTIF returns a number, not text, so it never repeats the word Yes; it only reports how many cells in the range match.

rw: SQL stands for Structured Query Language, the standard language for storing, retrieving and managing data in relational databases.

ww.System Quality Levels: SQL does not stand for System Quality Levels; that phrase does not name any database language, and SQL is the language used to query data.
ww.Simple Query Language: Simple Query Language is not the official name; SQL actually stands for Structured Query Language, and the word simple is not part of it.
ww.Secure Query Logic Set: Secure Query Logic Set is not a real expansion; SQL stands for Structured Query Language, and it is not defined by security features.

rw: SELECT retrieves data from a table, letting you choose which columns and rows to read without changing the stored data.

ww.Changes existing values: Changing existing values is done with UPDATE, not SELECT, which only reads data and leaves the table unchanged.
ww.Adds a new row to a table: Adding a new row is done with INSERT, not SELECT, which only retrieves data that is already stored in the table.
ww.Deletes a table permanently: Deleting a table is done with DROP, not SELECT, which is a read-only command that never removes a table.

rw: SELECT * returns all columns, FROM orders names the table, and WHERE total > 100 keeps only rows where the total is over 100.

ww.SELECT total FROM orders ORDER BY;: This query returns only the total column, has no filter for totals over 100, and has an incomplete ORDER BY clause, so it fails.
ww.INSERT INTO orders WHERE total > 100;: INSERT adds new rows and does not read existing ones; it also cannot use a WHERE filter in that form, so it does not return rows.
ww.DELETE FROM orders WHERE total > 100;: DELETE removes the matching rows from the table instead of returning them, so it does the opposite of what the question asks for.

rw: ORDER BY sorts the results by one or more columns, in ascending order by default or descending when you add DESC.

ww.Removes duplicates: Removing duplicates is done with DISTINCT, not ORDER BY, which changes the order of rows and keeps all of them.
ww.Counts the rows: Counting rows is done with COUNT, not ORDER BY, which only arranges the rows in a certain order.
ww.Joins two tables: Joining tables is done with JOIN, not ORDER BY, which only sorts rows and does not combine data from other tables.

rw: A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on related columns, such as a customer ID that appears in both tables.

ww.Renames a column in a table of data to a: Renaming a column is done with an alias or ALTER, not JOIN, which combines data from two tables using related columns.
ww.Sorts a single table of data by the date: Sorting a single table is the job of ORDER BY, while JOIN works with two tables and does not sort rows.
ww.Deletes the second table from the databa: JOIN does not delete anything; it only reads data, and deleting a table uses a different command such as DROP.

rw: Python is widely used for data science because of its readable syntax and strong libraries such as pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn.

ww.Latin: Latin is a human language used long ago and is not a programming language, so it cannot be used to analyze data.
ww.Braille: Braille is a tactile writing system for people with visual impairment, not a programming language, so it is not used for data science.
ww.Morse code: Morse code is a signaling system of dots and dashes, not a programming language, so it is not used in data science.

rw: A library is a collection of ready-made code that programmers can reuse, saving them from writing common functions from scratch.

ww.A file that deletes errors from the code: A library does not delete errors; the code inside it can have bugs, and using one does not automatically fix errors in a program.
ww.A screen that displays results of the pr: A screen that displays results is an output device, not a library, which is a package of reusable code.
ww.A building that stores books for readers: A building that stores books is a physical library, but in programming the term means reusable code, so this meaning is wrong here.

rw: Pandas is a Python library for working with tables of data, offering tools to load, clean, filter and summarize data frames.

ww.A library for drawing 3D video games on: Drawing 3D video games is the work of graphics engines, whereas pandas is a Python library for working with tables of data.
ww.A tool for sending emails to clients and: Sending email is the job of mail tools and libraries such as smtplib, not pandas, which is built for handling table data.
ww.A way to play music files on a computer: Playing music files is the job of audio software, not pandas, which is a library that handles tables of data.

rw: A Jupyter notebook is an interactive document that mixes code, results and text, so analysts can run code and explain findings in one place.

ww.A paper notebook for taking notes, with: A Jupyter notebook is software, not paper; it is an interactive document, so a ruled paper notebook does not describe it.
ww.A type of database server that stores ta: A database server stores records and answers queries, whereas a Jupyter notebook is a document that mixes code, results and text.
ww.A device that records lectures in a clas: A device that records lectures is hardware and has no connection to Jupyter, which is software for running code in a document.

rw: Data visualization software turns data into charts and dashboards, which makes patterns and trends easier to see and share with others.

ww.Writing legal contracts for a law firm: Writing legal contracts is done with word processors or legal tools, whereas data visualization software turns data into charts and dashboards.
ww.Encrypting passwords stored in a databas: Encrypting passwords is a security task, and visualization software does not encrypt anything; it displays data as charts and dashboards.
ww.Backing up files to the cloud each night: Backing up files to the cloud is the job of backup software, not visualization tools, which present data in charts.

rw: A dashboard shows key figures and charts on one screen at a glance, so people can monitor performance quickly without reading raw tables.

ww.A file that stores one number only on a: A file that stores one number only is simply a data file and does not display key figures and charts the way a dashboard does.
ww.A tool that cleans every error in the da: Cleaning every error in the data is done with data cleaning tools; a dashboard only shows information and does not fix mistakes.
ww.A list of all passwords used by the staf: A list of passwords is a security risk and is not a dashboard, which displays business figures and charts, not credentials.

rw: Cloud computing means using remote servers on the internet to store and process data instead of relying only on a local computer.

ww.Computing that needs no electricity or a: Cloud computing still needs electricity, since servers in data centers consume large amounts of power, so no-power computing is impossible.
ww.Computing that uses a single local machi: Using a single local machine in an office is traditional on-premises computing, and cloud computing instead uses remote servers.
ww.Computing that only works during bad wea: Cloud computing works in any weather; the word cloud is only a metaphor for the internet and has nothing to do with the sky.

rw: The cloud gives access to large computing power, such as many processors, without buying hardware, which suits AI projects that need heavy computation.

ww.Guaranteed removal of all costs for the: Costs do not disappear in the cloud, since you pay for usage, so a guaranteed removal of all costs is a false claim.
ww.No need for an internet link, as work is: Cloud work needs an internet link to reach the remote servers, so saying no internet is needed and work is local is wrong.
ww.Automatic accuracy of every result that: The cloud supplies computing resources but does not make results accurate, because accuracy depends on the data and the model.

rw: An API is a set of rules that lets different programs talk to each other, for example a weather service sending data to an app.

ww.A type of computer screen used to show g: A computer screen is a display device, whereas an API is a set of rules that lets programs talk to each other.
ww.A kind of database table that stores cus: A database table stores records and is not an API, which is an interface through which software requests and exchanges data.
ww.A tool for printing reports from a datab: Printing reports with headings is a reporting feature; an API instead defines how software components request and exchange data.

rw: A GPU runs many calculations in parallel, which speeds up the matrix math in AI and lets models be trained much faster than on a CPU.

ww.Storing the user's passwords in a secure: Storing passwords is done by a password manager or secure storage, and GPUs have no role as vaults for user credentials.
ww.Keeping time for the computer clock so f: Keeping time for the computer clock is the job of the system clock hardware, not the GPU, which does heavy calculations.
ww.Providing power to the monitor and other: Providing power to the monitor is the job of the power supply, whereas a GPU is a processor, so this answer is wrong.

rw: Version control tracks changes to code and files over time, so you can see who changed what and return to an earlier version.

ww.Controlling how fast a program runs on a: Controlling how fast a program runs is a performance setting and not version control, which tracks changes to code and files.
ww.Blocking unauthorized users from the net: Blocking unauthorized users from a network is done by firewalls and access controls, not version control, which records file history.
ww.Choosing the next release date for the t: Choosing the next release date is a project planning decision, and version control does not schedule anything; it records changes to files.

rw: Version control saves earlier versions of the files, so after a mistaken overwrite you can restore a previous version and recover the lost code.

ww.It rewrites the code automatically for y: Version control does not rewrite code automatically; it stores the history of changes so that people can choose what to restore.
ww.It deletes the teammate's account from t: Version control does not delete the teammate's account; that is an administrator action, and it works with files, not user accounts.
ww.It makes overwriting impossible, even by: Version control cannot prevent a person from overwriting a file by mistake, but it keeps history, so saying overwriting is impossible is false.

rw: Open-source software has publicly available code that anyone may use, study, modify and share, subject to its license terms.

ww.Software that runs only offline on a sin: Open-source software is not defined by running offline, since much of it runs on networks and online servers, so this definition is wrong.
ww.Software that cannot be changed by any u: Open-source software can be changed by users, because its code is open, so saying it cannot be changed is the opposite of the truth.
ww.Software that costs the most money, as t: Open-source software is often free and open to use, so it is not defined as the most expensive software, and cost is not the idea.
